paragraphs: A 3D recognition system can encounter objects outside the categories it learned during training. Standard closed-set evaluations largely leave this situation out, even though recognizing unfamiliar inputs matters for robots and autonomous systems. This paper studies semantic novelty detection on point clouds: identifying unfamiliar object categories from their three-dimensional geometry.

The authors introduce 3DOS, a benchmark with settings that become increasingly difficult in their category shifts. It includes synthetic-to-synthetic and real-to-real evaluation, as well as synthetic-to-real evaluation. This organization makes it possible to examine novelty detection both within a data domain and when the source of the data also changes.

The study also evaluates whether advances from 2D open-set recognition carry over to 3D inputs. Comparing several algorithms within a common benchmark reveals their respective strengths and limitations. The contribution is a shared basis for understanding and evaluating the problem, with findings that may guide methods designed specifically for 3D novelty detection.
neurips-2022-3dos-towards-3d-open-set-le.tldr: 3DOS benchmarks detection of unfamiliar categories in point clouds across category shifts and synthetic-to-real changes.

paragraphs: Vertical federated learning lets organizations collaborate when they hold different features about the same samples, without revealing their raw data. A practical obstacle is deciding which records correspond across organizations. Existing approaches often assume exact matches or select only the most similar record, potentially overlooking useful information in other plausible matches.

FedSim connects this record-linking process to model training. Its one-to-many linkage allows a record to be associated with multiple candidates, bringing record similarity into the learning procedure. This addresses a weakness of treating linkage as a fixed preliminary step: the training process otherwise has no way to provide feedback on those associations.

Experiments on eight datasets using different similarity measures show FedSim outperforming the compared state-of-the-art methods. The authors report benefits both for fuzzy identifiers and for traditional vertical federated learning tasks. They also theoretically analyze the additional privacy risk from sharing similarities, treating that information exchange as part of the method’s implications.
neurips-2022-a-coupled-design-of-exploit.tldr: FedSim integrates one-to-many record matching into vertical federated learning to improve predictions when record identities are uncertain.

paragraphs: This paper develops finite-sample guarantees for linear predictors with Gaussian inputs. Its main bound connects training error and Rademacher complexity, a measure of a predictor class’s flexibility, to test error measured through Moreau envelopes of the loss. These are transformed versions of the loss, and the result covers every continuous original loss.

The framework recovers an established optimistic rate for squared-loss linear regression and accommodates labels produced by potentially misspecified multi-index models. It also analyzes noisy interpolation for maximum-margin classifiers using squared hinge loss and establishes consistency in spiked-covariance settings. For Lipschitz losses, the bound improves the relevant contraction argument by a factor of two.

The authors additionally prove uniform convergence for interpolators under smooth, nonnegative losses. Using localized Gaussian width, they show the generalization bound will generally be sharp for empirical risk minimizers. The significance is a common finite-sample treatment that allows model misspecification and does not depend on a proportional relationship between growing sample size and dimension.
neurips-2022-a-non-asymptotic-moreau-env.tldr: A finite-sample theory bounds generalization for Gaussian-input linear predictors through Moreau envelopes, covering interpolation and model misspecification.

paragraphs: Few-shot classification must learn a new task from very few labeled examples, making performance sensitive to which examples happen to be available. The authors investigate this sample selection bias and find that it usually occurs when support examples lie near the task centroid, defined as the mean of the task’s class centers.

Their method, Task Centroid Projection Removing, transforms every image feature in the task by removing its component along the centroid direction. This simple geometric operation aims to prevent features from sitting too close to the task centroid. Because the small support set cannot accurately reveal the true centroid, the method estimates it using base features similar to individual support features.

Experiments across ten datasets from different domains show reliable classification improvements across multiple feature extractors and training algorithms. The findings suggest that part of few-shot sensitivity can be addressed directly in feature space. The proposed correction targets the identified geometry while accommodating the fact that the task center itself must be estimated from limited information.
neurips-2022-alleviating-the-sample-sele.tldr: Removing the feature component along an estimated task centroid improves few-shot classification across the evaluated datasets and methods.

paragraphs: Curriculum learning changes the order in which training examples are presented, but its benefits vary across settings. This paper investigates when that ordering helps using a simplified neural network task with a small number of informative features surrounded by many noisy ones. Statistical physics methods make the average learning trajectory analytically tractable in the high-dimensional limit.

The analysis finds a clear learning-speed benefit for curricula in the online setting. When training experiences can instead be stored and replayed, that advantage disappears for the standard networks studied. This difference offers an explanation for why curricula can appear valuable in some learning settings yet show little benefit in others.

The authors then introduce synaptic consolidation at transitions between curriculum stages, represented by a Gaussian prior connecting learning phases. They derive generalization performance as consolidation strength changes and show that this mechanism can substantially improve test performance. The results suggest that retaining earlier learning explicitly at stage boundaries may be important for fully benefiting from a curriculum.
neurips-2022-an-analytical-theory-of-cur.tldr: An analytical neural network model shows curriculum benefits depend on replay and can increase substantially with consolidation between learning stages.

paragraphs: This paper asks when iterative training algorithms that approximate local minima can generalize well. It assumes the population risk is strongly convex near its local minima, meaning the expected loss has sufficient curvature in those neighborhoods. This is weaker than requiring strong convexity or a suitable growth condition throughout the entire landscape.

For convex problems, the expected excess-risk bound decreases at a rate of approximately 1/n, with logarithmic factors suppressed. For nonconvex problems, that rate is maintained when the parameter-to-sample ratio stays below a specified threshold and the empirical risk has no spurious local minima with high probability. Without the latter assumption, the stated rate becomes approximately 1/√n.

The proofs combine algorithmic stability with analysis of the empirical loss landscape. Compared with earlier stability-based results, the bounds are insensitive to dimension and avoid restrictions on implementation, learning rate, or iteration count. These conclusions still concern proper iterative algorithms under the stated landscape conditions; they explain how local curvature can support generalization even in nonconvex, high-dimensional problems.
neurips-2022-characterization-of-excess-.tldr: Local strong convexity supports generalization bounds for iterative learning, with faster nonconvex rates under additional landscape and dimension-to-sample conditions.

paragraphs: Code generation models are often trained to reproduce reference programs from natural-language descriptions. This leaves useful evidence in unit tests underused: matching a reference is only one route to learning whether a generated program actually works. CodeRL brings functional-correctness feedback into both training and generation through reinforcement learning.

During training, the language model acts as an actor that generates programs. A separate critic learns to predict their functional correctness and supplies dense feedback to the actor. At inference time, a critical sampling procedure uses example unit-test results and critic scores to guide automatic program regeneration. The framework also extends CodeT5 with revised learning objectives, larger models, and improved pretraining data.

The authors report state-of-the-art results on APPS and strong zero-shot transfer to MBPP, where they also report state-of-the-art results. These findings support combining pretrained code models with correctness-oriented feedback. The approach makes execution-related signals useful beyond a final pass-or-fail assessment by incorporating them into how programs are learned and regenerated.
neurips-2022-coderl-mastering-code-gener.tldr: CodeRL improves code generation by training with a correctness critic and regenerating programs using unit-test feedback and critic scores.

paragraphs: Unsupervised distribution alignment learns transformations that bring samples from different source distributions into a shared distribution. It appears in generative modeling, domain adaptation, and socially aware learning. Many existing methods use adversarial optimization, where one component minimizes an objective while another maximizes it, making both optimization and evaluation challenging.

This paper unifies and extends approaches based on invertible transformations within a non-adversarial framework. The authors prove that the proposed formulation is equivalent to minimizing an upper bound on Jensen-Shannon divergence, a measure of distributional difference. Its optimization is cooperative: the participating components minimize rather than compete over the objective.

The framework also supplies a natural evaluation measure for unsupervised alignment and addresses limitations in efficiently aligning multiple distributions. Experiments on simulated and real-world data demonstrate benefits of the approach. The theoretical connection matters because it gives the cooperative objective a distribution-comparison interpretation, joining optimization and evaluation within one formulation instead of leaving them as separate design choices.
neurips-2022-cooperative-distribution-al.tldr: A unified invertible-transformation framework aligns distributions cooperatively by minimizing an upper bound on Jensen-Shannon divergence.

paragraphs: Strong predictive performance on an available EEG dataset may not reveal how a model will behave under changes encountered in practice. This study develops diagnostics intended to expose potential problems before deployment without requiring an external dataset. It focuses on changes to electrophysiological signals that can be modeled through realistic data transformations.

The evaluation examines more than downstream task performance. It also studies the model’s latent space, the internal representation produced from EEG inputs, and its predictive uncertainty after the transformations. These additional views ask whether the learned representation remains intact and how confidence behaves when the input distribution changes.

The authors test multiple EEG feature encoders on two clinically relevant tasks using large public clinical EEG datasets. Within those experiments, latent-space integrity and uncertainty measures under the proposed shifts appear useful for anticipating performance degradation. The finding supports their potential as predeployment diagnostics, while remaining a qualified result tied to the transformations, models, and tasks studied.
neurips-2022-evaluating-latent-space-rob.tldr: EEG transformations reveal representation and uncertainty changes that may help anticipate deployment-time performance degradation without external data.

paragraphs: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo generates candidate samples by simulating motion through a target probability distribution. Conventionally, a trajectory runs for a fixed simulation time. This paper changes the stopping rule: Fixed-Distance HMC stops after a fixed distance has been traveled. The authors find that this mechanism tends to propose points with higher target probability.

The method is paired with a naturally associated momentum distribution that is non-Gaussian. It produces momenta with larger expected magnitude while keeping proposal acceptance probability close to one. Together, the distance-based trajectories and momentum choice translate into less correlation between consecutive states of the sampling chain.

Experiments show improvements over baseline HMC and No-U-Turn sampling in effective sample size per gradient evaluation. This measure relates the amount of useful sampling information to a central computational cost. The reported benefit therefore concerns sampling efficiency, rather than simply generating more proposals. The findings support fixed traversed distance as a useful alternative trajectory rule in the settings evaluated.
neurips-2022-fixed-distance-hamiltonian-.tldr: Fixed-Distance HMC changes trajectory stopping and momentum sampling to improve effective sample size per gradient in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Concept-based models make predictions through a vocabulary of high-level concepts, with the aim of making their reasoning understandable. That goal depends on each learned concept actually carrying its intended meaning. The authors argue that existing heuristic approaches lack a clear account of interpretability and can learn representations whose semantics do not match the concepts they are supposed to express.

The paper defines interpretability through alignment between the model’s representation and an underlying process that generates the data. GlanceNets pursue this alignment by combining techniques from disentangled representation learning and open-set recognition. This gives concept learning an explicit target: correspondence with the relevant factors of data generation.

With concept-level supervision, GlanceNets achieve better alignment than the compared state-of-the-art approaches while preventing unintended spurious information from leaking into learned concepts. This matters because a concept representation can otherwise carry information beyond its stated meaning. The findings connect interpretability to the content of the representation, with concept supervision forming part of the demonstrated setup.
neurips-2022-glancenets-interpretable-le.tldr: GlanceNets use concept supervision, disentangled representations, and open-set recognition to improve semantic alignment and prevent unintended information leakage.

paragraphs: Graph transformers must choose which nodes to consider, especially when graphs are large. This paper identifies two weaknesses in existing choices: sampling often ignores graph characteristics and changes during training, and it tends to concentrate on nearby nodes. Synthetic-data experiments show that these sampling strategies can be suboptimal.

The proposed method treats node sampling as an adversarial bandit problem. Rewards depend on attention weights and can change as training progresses, allowing sampling decisions to respond to the learning process. A second component introduces hierarchical attention with graph coarsening, representing the graph at a coarser level to capture interactions over longer distances while reducing computational complexity.

Experiments on real-world datasets show the method outperforming the evaluated graph transformers and popular graph neural networks. Its contribution combines adaptive selection with a hierarchy for distant interactions. These components address complementary issues: which nodes receive attention during learning, and how the model can represent relationships that extend beyond a local neighborhood.
neurips-2022-hierarchical-graph-transfor.tldr: Adaptive node sampling and hierarchical attention improve graph transformer performance while supporting longer-range interactions at lower computational complexity.

paragraphs: An unsupervised representation can be useful while still leaving uncertainty about how stable or reliable it is. This paper addresses the absence or poor calibration of uncertainty estimates in established representation-learning methods. It introduces a Bayesian autoencoder that learns representations together with uncertainty in both the latent representation and the output.

Training maximizes a new variational lower bound on the autoencoder evidence using Monte Carlo expectation-maximization. The variational distribution has the form of a Laplace approximation. To make this approach workable for high-dimensional data, the authors develop a Hessian approximation whose scaling is linear in data size, addressing a computational obstacle in the uncertainty calculation.

Empirically, the Laplacian autoencoder produces well-calibrated uncertainty estimates in latent and output spaces. The authors also demonstrate improved performance across multiple downstream tasks. The findings connect the reliability of uncertainty estimates to practical representation quality: accounting for uncertainty is useful both for assessing learned features and for the later tasks that consume them.
neurips-2022-laplacian-autoencoders-for-.tldr: A Bayesian autoencoder uses Laplace-shaped uncertainty approximations to improve uncertainty calibration and downstream performance.

paragraphs: Learning reusable skills from previous experiences can help reinforcement-learning agents solve new tasks faster. A common approach treats skills as latent variables and chooses them to maximize the likelihood of recorded experience. The problem is that many different skill decompositions can explain the same experience equally well, including degenerate decompositions.

This paper adds a description-length penalty to the likelihood objective. The penalty encourages skills to capture structures shared across experiences, giving the learning process a reason to prefer some decompositions over equally likely alternatives. Compression therefore serves as an additional criterion for deciding what a useful skill should represent.

In the reported experiments, skills learned with the combined objective solve downstream tasks using fewer samples than skills learned through likelihood alone. The objective also scales to challenging tasks with high-dimensional image observations, extending beyond the low-dimensional observations emphasized in much prior offline multitask work. The results suggest that fitting past behavior benefits from an explicit preference for reusable common structure.
neurips-2022-learning-options-via-compre.tldr: Adding a description-length penalty to skill learning encourages shared structure and reduces samples needed for downstream reinforcement-learning tasks.

paragraphs: In repeated first-price auctions, a bidder must decide how much to bid when simply bidding their private value is no longer optimal. This paper studies how predictions about competitors can help that decision. It allows the highest competing bid to vary adversarially over time, avoiding assumptions about a regular pattern in competitors’ behavior.

The bidder instead receives a hint from a black-box machine-learning model. The authors analyze two versions: a single predicted competing bid, and an interval representing a confidence region for that bid. They establish minimax-optimal regret bounds for both, characterizing the best achievable worst-case performance within the respective settings.

The two hint formats produce quantitatively different regret behavior, showing that the form of predictive information matters. Additional sparsity structure in competitors’ maximum bids permits improved bounds. Demonstrations using real bidding data complement the theoretical analysis. Together, the results explain how learned predictions can support adaptive bidding even when the competing sequence itself is not assumed to be predictable.
neurips-2022-leveraging-the-hints-adapti.tldr: The paper establishes optimal regret guarantees for first-price bidding with point or interval predictions of potentially adversarial competing bids.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning is usually assessed by testing learned features on selected downstream tasks. This paper asks a different question: if data arise from a parametric probabilistic model, can an optimal self-supervised predictor reveal the parameters that generated those data? This perspective evaluates what the prediction task identifies about the data distribution itself.

The authors study masked prediction for sequential latent-variable models, specifically Hidden Markov Models with discrete or conditionally Gaussian observations. They assume a suitable parametric form for the predictor and analyze its optimum. The central question is whether the generative model’s parameters can be extracted from the optimal predictor’s parameters.

The results show that identifiability depends on task difficulty, which is shaped by both the data model and the number of tokens being predicted. The analysis connects this question to uniqueness of tensor rank decompositions, a tool used in moment-based identifiability arguments. This provides a theoretical way to examine how masking-task design affects recoverable information, beyond performance on a chosen downstream benchmark.
neurips-2022-masked-prediction-a-paramet.tldr: For specified Hidden Markov Models, masked-prediction task difficulty determines whether an optimal predictor identifies the underlying generative parameters.

paragraphs: Implicit graph neural networks were introduced to capture relationships across long distances in a graph. This paper argues that their practical reach remains limited and that they also struggle to represent graph information at multiple resolutions. These weaknesses constrain what the models can express despite their intended ability to go beyond nearby nodes.

The authors theoretically connect the effective range of earlier implicit models to convergence of the iterative equations they use. This links long-distance information capture to the behavior of the underlying computation. They then propose MGNNI, a graph neural network with implicit layers that models structures at multiple scales and expands the effective range of dependencies it can capture.

Experiments on node classification and whole-graph classification show MGNNI outperforming representative baselines. The evaluations also indicate improved multiscale modeling and stronger capture of long-range dependencies. The contribution combines an explanation of why previous implicit models have limited reach with an architecture designed to address both distance and resolution.
neurips-2022-mgnni-multiscale-graph-neur.tldr: MGNNI expands the effective reach of implicit graph networks and models multiple graph scales, improving the evaluated classification tasks.

paragraphs: Regularization introduces preferences about how a model should behave to help it generalize beyond training examples. This paper investigates a preference at the level of individual neurons: how consistently a neuron responds to examples belonging to the same class. The authors analyze these class-dependent response distributions as a source of inductive bias.

Their Neuron Steadiness Hypothesis proposes that similar responses within a class lead to better generalization. Neuron Steadiness Regularization implements this idea by reducing the variance of each neuron’s responses among same-class examples. The paper also provides a theoretical guarantee for the method’s generalization benefit based on a complexity measure.

Experiments cover multilayer perceptrons, convolutional networks, and graph neural networks across benchmark datasets from different domains. The regularized versions consistently outperform their unregularized counterparts in those experiments, with significant gains and little additional computation. The findings support neuron-level response consistency as a useful regularization target across the evaluated model families.
neurips-2022-neuron-with-steady-response.tldr: Neuron Steadiness Regularization reduces within-class response variance and improves generalization across the tested neural network families.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can gain expressive power by examining subgraphs, but the relationships among these architectures have been difficult to characterize. This paper introduces a common theoretical framework for studying them and connects their capabilities to the Weisfeiler-Leman hierarchy, an established reference for distinguishing graph structures.

Within this framework, the authors show that increasing subgraph size always increases expressive power. Their analysis also clarifies limitations through relationships to the k-WL hierarchy. Alongside these theoretical questions, they examine how a model should choose subgraphs, since existing methods often enumerate all subgraphs of a size, sample uniformly, or rely on hand-designed rules.

The proposed data-driven approaches learn to sample subgraphs using methods that support backpropagation through complex discrete probability distributions. On standard benchmarks, the learned approaches improve prediction accuracy while reducing computation time relative to subgraph-enhanced networks without data-driven selection. The work therefore joins a clearer account of representational power with evidence that selective, learned use of subgraphs can improve practical efficiency.
neurips-2022-ordered-subgraph-aggregatio.tldr: A unified theory characterizes subgraph network expressivity, while learned subgraph sampling improves benchmark accuracy and computation time.

paragraphs: Self-supervised visual learning often treats differently augmented versions of one image as semantically related. Aggressive transformations increase training diversity, but they can alter image structure enough that the paired views no longer share meaning. RSA addresses this semantic shift by changing the balance between weakly and aggressively augmented pairs during training.

The method treats semantically inconsistent pairs as a noisy minority. Its weighting schedule draws on the tendency of neural networks to learn clean majority examples before overfitting noisy ones. Aggressive pairs receive relatively large weights early in training, then gradually smaller weights as training progresses and fitting noisy pairs becomes a concern.

With ResNet-50 trained for 200 epochs, the reported ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy is 73.1%, a 2.5% improvement over BYOL as stated by the authors. Additional experiments show good transfer to downstream tasks. The results support retaining the diversity of aggressive augmentation while adjusting its influence over time to reduce the harm from semantically inconsistent pairs.
neurips-2022-rsa-reducing-semantic-shift.tldr: RSA gradually reduces the weight of aggressive augmentation pairs to limit semantic-shift noise while preserving their early training benefits.

paragraphs: Molecular optimization searches for molecules with desirable properties, but evaluating candidates consumes a limited resource. This paper emphasizes sample efficiency: how many molecules an algorithm must submit to the evaluation oracle. It argues that comparisons based on trivial or individually designed tasks make progress difficult to assess, especially when evaluation budgets are overlooked.

The authors introduce Practical Molecular Optimization, an open-source benchmark with a standardized experimental setup. They compare 25 molecular design algorithms across 23 tasks, each optimizing a single scalar objective. A central evaluation setting limits algorithms to 10,000 oracle queries, making the cost of finding good candidates explicit.

Under this budget, most methods described as state of the art fail to outperform their predecessors, and some benchmark problems remain unsolved efficiently by the evaluated algorithms. The study also examines optimization choices, molecule assembly strategies, and oracle landscapes. These results show why practical comparisons need to consider how quickly an algorithm improves, alongside the quality of molecules it eventually finds.
neurips-2022-sample-efficiency-matters-a.tldr: PMO compares molecular optimization under limited evaluation budgets and finds that many newer methods do not outperform earlier ones.

paragraphs: Mental state decoding aims to identify states such as anger or joy from brain activity. This paper investigates whether self-supervised learning can prepare models for that task by first learning from a broad collection of neuroimaging data. Its frameworks adapt ideas from language modeling to sequences of brain activity.

The central approach models how activity evolves over time, treating activity sequences in a way analogous to text sequences. The authors pretrain on functional magnetic resonance imaging data comprising 11,980 experimental runs from 1,726 individuals across 34 datasets. They then adapt the pretrained models to benchmark datasets for mental state decoding.

The pretrained models transfer well and generally outperform baseline models trained from scratch. Among the self-supervised frameworks studied, the one based on causal language modeling clearly performs best. These results support learning brain dynamics from broad data before specializing to a decoding task, while also showing that the choice of sequence-learning framework makes a meaningful difference in the evaluated setting.
neurips-2022-self-supervised-learning-of.tldr: Self-supervised pretraining on broad fMRI data improves mental state decoding, with causal language modeling performing best among the tested frameworks.

paragraphs: Accurate 3D object detectors can require substantial computation. This paper studies knowledge distillation for pillar- and voxel-based detectors, training smaller students with guidance from stronger teachers. It first examines model compression and reduced input resolution to construct students with useful accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs, then benchmarks existing 2D distillation methods on six teacher-student pairs.

The proposed pipeline improves distillation in two ways. It transfers prediction information only at a few pivotal positions selected using the teacher’s classification responses. It also initializes students through teacher-guided weight inheritance, helping pass along the teacher’s feature-extraction ability. These choices target both the information transferred during training and the student’s starting point.

On Waymo, the best-performing model reaches 65.75% LEVEL 2 mAPH, exceeding its teacher while using 44% of the teacher’s floating-point operations. A separate most-efficient model runs at 51 frames per second on an NVIDIA A100, 2.2 times faster than PointPillar with higher accuracy. These results demonstrate favorable tradeoffs across distinct student configurations.
neurips-2022-towards-efficient-3d-object.tldr: Selective distillation and teacher-guided initialization produce 3D detectors with strong accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs on Waymo.

paragraphs: Speech models that combine audio and visual information can be accurate and robust, but paired data are scarce and maintaining separate models for each input modality adds deployment cost. u-HuBERT addresses both issues through a unified self-supervised pretraining framework that can use multimodal speech alongside data containing only one modality.

The framework uses a shared masked cluster prediction objective and modality dropout during pretraining. This trains a common model while varying which modalities are available. The authors show that a single fine-tuned model can match or exceed state-of-the-art models specialized for individual modalities, supporting unified processing of audio, video, and their combination.

A model fine-tuned using only audio also performs well with visual and audiovisual speech inputs across multiple speech-processing tasks. This is zero-shot transfer across fine-tuning modalities. On LRS3, the single model achieves word error rates of 1.2% for audiovisual input, 1.4% for audio, and 27.2% for visual input, demonstrating distinct capabilities within one model.
neurips-2022-u-hubert-unified-mixed-moda.tldr: u-HuBERT unifies mixed-modality speech pretraining and enables audio-only fine-tuning to transfer to visual and audiovisual inputs.

paragraphs: An image classifier’s uncertainty is useful both when an input comes from an unfamiliar distribution and when its prediction is wrong. UQGAN targets both situations within an approach to aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. The paper broadens the focus of GAN-based uncertainty training beyond detecting out-of-distribution examples alone.

Instead of surrounding the entire training distribution with generated unfamiliar examples, the method treats each class separately. A conditional generative adversarial network creates out-of-class examples to shield individual classes, and a one-versus-all classifier complements this training. This changes the organization of generated examples from a single overall boundary to class-specific boundaries.

Experiments, particularly on CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and Tiny ImageNet, show improved detection of out-of-distribution inputs and false positives compared with state-of-the-art GAN-trained classifiers. The generated examples do not significantly change calibration error and yield a significant accuracy improvement. The results support class-conditional generation as a way to improve error and novelty detection while also strengthening classification performance in the tested settings.
neurips-2022-uqgan-a-unified-model-for-u.tldr: UQGAN generates class-specific out-of-class examples to improve detection of unfamiliar inputs and false positives while increasing classification accuracy.
